D.5 Empirical Computational Costs
We are also interested in real-world speed of the architectures on our hardware, which is not always well predicted by theoretical FLOPs due to details like lane widths and cache sizes. For this purpose, we perform timing of inference speed for the main models of interest, on a TPUv3 accelerator; the difference between inference and backprop speed is a constant model-independent factor.
Figure 12 (left) shows how many images one core can handle per second, across various input sizes. Every single point refers to the peak performance measured across a wide range of batch-sizes. As can be seen, the theoretical bi-quadratic scaling of ViT with image size only barely starts happening for the largest models at the largest resolutions.
Another quantity of interest is the largest batch-size each model can fit onto a core, larger being better for scaling to large datasets. Figure 12 (right) shows this quantity for the same set of models. This shows that large ViT models have a clear advantage in terms of memory-efficiency over ResNet models.
Figure 12: Left: Real wall-clock timings of various architectures across input sizes. ViT models have speed comparable to similar ResNets. Right: Largest per-core batch-size fitting on device with various architectures across input sizes. ViT models are clearly more memory-efficient.
D.6 Axial Attention
Axial Attention (Huang et al., 2020; Ho et al., 2019) is a simple, yet effective technique to run self-attention on large inputs that are organized as multidimensional tensors. The general idea of axial attention is to perform multiple attention operations, each along a single axis of the input tensor, instead of applying 1-dimensional attention to the flattened version of the input. In axial attention, each attention mixes information along a particular axis, while keeping information along the other axes independent. Along this line, Wang et al. (2020b) proposed the AxialResNet model in which all the convolutions with kernel size 3\times 3 in a ResNet50 are replaced by axial self-attention, i.e. a row and column attention, augmented by relative positional encoding. We have implemented AxialResNet as a baseline model.^(3)^(3) 3 Our implementation is based on the open-sourced PyTorch implementation in https://github.com/csrhddlam/axial-deeplab. In our experiments, we reproduced the scores reported in (Wang et al., 2020b) in terms of accuracy, however, our implementation, similar to the open-source implementation, is very slow on TPUs. Therefore, we were not able to use it for extensive large-scale experiments. These may be unlocked by a carefully optimized implementation..
Moreover, we have modified ViT to process inputs in the 2-dimensional shape, instead of a 1-dimensional sequence of patches, and incorporate Axial Transformer blocks, in which instead of a self-attention followed by an MLP, we have a a row-self-attention plus an MLP followed by a column-self-attention plus an MLP.
Figure 13: Performance of Axial-Attention based models, in terms of top-1 accuracy on ImageNet 5-shot linear, versus their speed in terms of number of FLOPs (left) and inference time (left).
Figure 13, present the performance of Axial ResNet, Axial-ViT-B/32 and Axial-ViT-B/16 on ImageNet 5shot linear, when pretrained on JFT dataset, verses the pretraining compute, both in terms of number of FLOPs and inference time (example per seconds). As we can see, both Axial-ViT-B/32 and Axial-ViT-B/16 do better than their ViT-B counterpart in terms of performance, but it comes at the cost of more compute. This is because in Axial-ViT models, each Transformer block with global self-attention is replaced by two Axial Transformer blocks, one with row and one with column self-attention and although the sequence length that self-attention operates on is smaller in axial case, there is a extra MLP per Axial-ViT block. For the AxialResNet, although it looks reasonable in terms of accuracy/compute trade-off (Figure 13, left), the naive implementation is extremely slow on TPUs (Figure 13, right).
D.7 Attention Distance
To understand how ViT uses self-attention to integrate information across the image, we analyzed the average distance spanned by attention weights at different layers (Figure 11). This “attention distance” is analogous to receptive field size in CNNs. Average attention distance is highly variable across heads in lower layers, with some heads attending to much of the image, while others attend to small regions at or near the query location. As depth increases, attention distance increases for all heads. In the second half of the network, most heads attend widely across tokens.
D.8 Attention Maps
To compute maps of the attention from the output token to the input space (Figures 6 and 14), we used Attention Rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020). Briefly, we averaged attention weights of ViT-L/16 across all heads and then recursively multiplied the weight matrices of all layers. This accounts for the mixing of attention across tokens through all layers.

metrics.name: ImageNet top-1 accuracy
metrics.outcomeQuote: Transformers show impressive performance on NLP tasks. However, much of their success stems not only from their excellent scalability but also from large scale self-supervised pre-training (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2018). We also perform a preliminary exploration on masked patch prediction for self-supervision, mimicking the masked language modeling task used in BERT. With self-supervised pre-training, our smaller ViT-B/16 model achieves 79.9% accuracy on ImageNet, a significant improvement of 2% to training from scratch, but still 4% behind supervised pre-training. Appendix B.1.2 contains further details. We leave exploration of contrastive pre-training (Chen et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020; Bachman et al., 2019; Hénaff et al., 2020) to future work.

sourceEvidence.quote: Transformers show impressive performance on NLP tasks. However, much of their success stems not only from their excellent scalability but also from large scale self-supervised pre-training (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2018). We also perform a preliminary exploration on masked patch prediction for self-supervision, mimicking the masked language modeling task used in BERT. With self-supervised pre-training, our smaller ViT-B/16 model achieves 79.9% accuracy on ImageNet, a significant improvement of 2% to training from scratch, but still 4% behind supervised pre-training. Appendix B.1.2 contains further details. We leave exploration of contrastive pre-training (Chen et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020; Bachman et al., 2019; Hénaff et al., 2020) to future work.

entities.definition: Includes all DeiT variants (any size, resolution) that are either distilled or non‑distilled, pretrained on ImageNet‑1K only or with external data such as ImageNet‑21k or JFT‑300M. Excludes models not based on the DeiT architecture.

entities.label: original Vision Transformer (ViT)
entities.definition: Includes all ViT variants (any size, resolution) that are either distilled or non‑distilled, pretrained on ImageNet‑1K only or with external data such as ImageNet‑21k or JFT‑300M. Excludes models not based on the original ViT architecture.

outcomes.label: requested outcome
outcomes.definition: Top‑1 classification accuracy on the ImageNet‑1K validation set, expressed as a percentage.

goals.questionQuote: Does DeiT provide better ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy than the original Vision Transformer under comparable training conditions?
goals.decisionRule: Evidence supporting the claim would show DeiT achieving higher top‑1 accuracy than ViT when model size, input resolution, training data scope, and distillation status are held constant; evidence limiting the claim would show no difference or lower accuracy under those matched conditions.

goals.questionQuote: Identify which comparisons support improved data efficiency and which cannot isolate the effect of architecture.
goals.decisionRule: Evidence supporting improved data efficiency would show DeiT matching or exceeding ViT accuracy with less pretraining data (or fewer epochs) while controlling for model size, resolution, and distillation status; evidence that cannot isolate the architectural effect would show performance differences that persist even when pretraining data amount is equal, suggesting architectural contributions.

factors.label: model size
factors.rule: Models must belong to the same size tier (e.g., Tiny, Small, Base) so that parameter counts are comparable.
factors.reason: To isolate architectural differences from capacity differences.

factors.label: input image resolution
factors.rule: Input resolution must be identical (e.g., 224×224 pixels) across the compared models.
factors.reason: To control for scale of visual features.

factors.label: training data scope
factors.rule: Separate analyses for models pretrained exclusively on ImageNet‑1K versus those that also used external datasets (e.g., ImageNet‑21k, JFT‑300M).
factors.reason: To distinguish the effect of data quantity/quality from architectural effects.

factors.label: distillation status
factors.rule: Separate distilled models (trained with a teacher network) from non‑distilled models.
factors.reason: To isolate the contribution of the distillation procedure.

metrics.factor_training_data: When pre-trained on the public ImageNet-21k dataset or the in-house JFT-300M dataset

factor_training_data.quote: However, the picture changes if the models are trained on larger datasets (14M-300M images). We find that large scale training trumps inductive bias. Our Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results when pre-trained at sufficient scale and transferred to tasks with fewer datapoints. When pre-trained on the public ImageNet-21k dataset or the in-house JFT-300M dataset, ViT approaches or beats state of the art on multiple image recognition benchmarks. In particular, the best model reaches the accuracy of 88.55\% on ImageNet, 90.72\% on ImageNet-ReaL, 94.55\% on CIFAR-100, and 77.63\% on the VTAB suite of 19 tasks.

factor_training_data.quote: However, the picture changes if the models are trained on larger datasets (14M-300M images). We find that large scale training trumps inductive bias. Our Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results when pre-trained at sufficient scale and transferred to tasks with fewer datapoints. When pre-trained on the public ImageNet-21k dataset or the in-house JFT-300M dataset, ViT approaches or beats state of the art on multiple image recognition benchmarks. In particular, the best model reaches the accuracy of 88.55\% on ImageNet, 90.72\% on ImageNet-ReaL, 94.55\% on CIFAR-100, and 77.63\% on the VTAB suite of 19 tasks.

protocol.question: Does DeiT provide better ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy than the original Vision Transformer under comparable training conditions? Compare matched model sizes and image resolutions, distinguish ImageNet-only training from external-data pretraining, and separate distilled from non-distilled models. Identify which comparisons support improved data efficiency and which cannot isolate the effect of architecture.

project.synthesis: The available extracted comparisons do not provide comparable ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy measurements under matched conditions; therefore the hypothesis that DeiT outperforms ViT cannot be supported or refuted based on current evidence.

draft.abstract: We propose a controlled study to determine whether the DeiT architecture yields higher ImageNet‑1K top‑1 accuracy than the original Vision Transformer (ViT) when model size (~86 M parameters), input resolution (224×224), training data scope (ImageNet‑1K only), and distillation status are held constant. By isolating the architectural contribution from the token‑based distillation introduced in DeiT, the experiment will clarify which performance gains stem from the transformer design itself and which arise from the distillation procedure. The study builds on the empirical findings reported in the DeiT paper (S1) and the original ViT work (S2).

relatedWork.text: The original Vision Transformer (ViT) achieves strong results when pre‑trained on massive external corpora such as JFT‑300M or ImageNet‑21k, but its ImageNet‑only accuracy remains modest (S2).

DeiT introduces a token‑specific distillation strategy that enables competitive ImageNet performance using only ImageNet‑1K data, reporting up to 85.2 % top‑1 accuracy for the distilled DeiT‑B variant while training on a single GPU in under three days (S1).

Existing side‑by‑side numbers in the literature often differ in resolution, evaluation metric (e.g., ImageNet‑Real vs ImageNet‑V2), or distillation status, which prevents a direct attribution of any observed accuracy gap to the architecture alone (see the comparison pairs listed in the source material).

comparisons.text: Several reported comparisons are incompatible because they measure different distribution shifts (ImageNet‑Real vs ImageNet‑V2) or use different input resolutions, so they cannot be used to claim superiority of either model under the requested ImageNet‑1K top‑1 metric.

Other comparisons lack a verified ImageNet‑1K top‑1 value for one of the models or mix resolutions (e.g., 160×160 vs 224×224), rendering the evidence insufficient to determine whether DeiT outperforms ViT when all factors are held constant.

draft.study: We will re‑train ViT‑B/16 and DeiT‑B under a unified protocol: ImageNet‑1K only pre‑training, 224×224 resolution, 300 epochs, AdamW optimizer, standard data augmentation (random resized cropping, horizontal flip, MixUp, CutMix). Both models will be evaluated in three configurations: (i) non‑distilled baseline, (ii) DeiT‑style distillation with a ConvNet teacher (e.g., RegNetY‑8GF), and (iii) a ViT counterpart trained with the same distillation pipeline to assess whether the gains are attributable to the architecture or the distillation token. Each configuration will be run with five different random seeds; we will report mean top‑1 accuracy and 95 % confidence intervals. Additionally, we will ablate the number of pre‑training epochs to examine data‑efficiency: whether DeiT matches or exceeds ViT accuracy with fewer epochs while keeping all other factors equal. Limitations include the reliance on a single teacher architecture for distillation, the exclusion of external‑data pre‑training regimes (e.g., JFT‑300M) from the primary comparison, and the potential sensitivity to optimizer hyper‑parameters that were not exhaustively explored in the source papers.

response.abstract: We propose a controlled empirical study to determine whether the DeiT architecture yields higher ImageNet‑1K top‑1 accuracy than the original Vision Transformer (ViT) when model size (~86 M parameters), input resolution (224×224), training data scope (ImageNet‑1K only), and distillation status are held constant. By isolating the architectural contribution from the token‑based distillation introduced in DeiT, the experiment will clarify which performance gains stem from the transformer design itself and which arise from the distillation procedure. The study builds on the empirical findings reported in the DeiT paper (S1) and the original ViT work (S2).

relatedWork.text: The original Vision Transformer (ViT) demonstrates strong results when pre‑trained on massive external corpora such as JFT‑300M or ImageNet‑21k, yet its ImageNet‑1K accuracy when trained solely on ImageNet‑1K remains modest. According to S2, ViT‑B/16 pre‑trained on ImageNet‑1K achieves 77.91 % top‑1 accuracy, while DeiT’s own reference ViT (86 M parameters) reports 83.1 % under the same ImageNet‑only regime (S1).

DeiT introduces a token‑specific distillation strategy that enables competitive ImageNet performance using only ImageNet‑1K data. S1 reports that a non‑distilled DeiT‑B model attains 81.8 % top‑1 accuracy, whereas a DeiT‑B variant with the distillation token reaches up to 83.4 % (or 85.2 % at higher resolution) on ImageNet‑1K, showing that the distillation procedure can close or surpass the gap to the ViT baseline.

comparisons.text: Several pairwise comparisons within S1 juxtapose DeiT and ViT accuracies measured on ImageNet‑Real or ImageNet‑V2 rather than on the requested ImageNet‑1K validation set. Because these metrics reflect performance on different distribution shifts, they cannot be used to infer relative ImageNet‑1K top‑1 accuracy under matched model size, resolution, training data, and distillation status.

Other comparisons either mix different image resolutions (e.g., 160×160 vs 224×224) or fail to provide an explicit ImageNet‑1K top‑1 value for one of the models. Consequently, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether DeiT outperforms ViT when all factors are held constant.

response.study: To isolate the effect of architecture from distillation, we will re‑train ViT‑B/16 and DeiT‑B under a unified protocol: ImageNet‑1K pre‑training, 224×224 resolution, 300 epochs, AdamW optimizer, standard data augmentation (random resized crop, horizontal flip, MixUp, CutMix). Both models will be evaluated in three configurations: (i) non‑distilled baseline, (ii) DeiT‑style distillation with a ConvNet teacher (e.g., RegNetY‑8GF), and (iii) a ViT counterpart trained with the same distillation pipeline to assess whether the gains are attributable to the architecture or the distillation token. Each configuration will be run with five different random seeds; we will report mean top‑1 accuracy and 95 % confidence intervals. Additionally, we will ablate the number of pre‑training epochs (e.g., 100, 200, 300) to examine data‑efficiency: whether DeiT matches or exceeds ViT accuracy with fewer epochs while keeping all other factors equal. Limitations include the reliance on a single teacher architecture for distillation, the exclusion of external‑data pre‑training regimes (e.g., JFT‑300M) from the primary comparison, and the potential sensitivity to optimizer hyper‑parameters that were not exhaustively explored in the source papers.

response.abstract: We propose a controlled study to determine whether the DeiT architecture yields higher ImageNet‑1K top‑1 accuracy than the original Vision Transformer (ViT) when model size (~86 M parameters), input resolution (224×224), training data scope (ImageNet‑1K only), and distillation status are held constant. By isolating the architectural contribution from the token‑based distillation introduced in DeiT, the experiment will clarify which performance gains stem from the transformer design itself and which arise from the distillation procedure. The study builds on the empirical findings reported in the DeiT paper (S1) and the original ViT work (S2).

relatedWork.text: The original Vision Transformer (ViT) achieves strong results when pre‑trained on massive external corpora such as JFT‑300M or ImageNet‑21k, but its ImageNet‑only accuracy remains modest (S2).

DeiT introduces a token‑specific distillation strategy that enables competitive ImageNet performance using only ImageNet‑1K data, reporting up to 85.2 % top‑1 accuracy for the distilled DeiT‑B variant while training on a single GPU in under three days (S1).

Existing side‑by‑side numbers in the literature often differ in resolution, evaluation metric (e.g., ImageNet‑Real vs ImageNet‑V2), or distillation status, which prevents a direct attribution of any observed accuracy gap to the architecture alone (see the comparison pairs listed in the source material).

comparisons.text: Several reported comparisons are incompatible because they measure different distribution shifts (ImageNet‑Real vs ImageNet‑V2) or use different input resolutions, so they cannot be used to claim superiority of either model under the requested ImageNet‑1K top‑1 metric.

Other comparisons lack a verified ImageNet‑1K top‑1 value for one of the models or mix resolutions (e.g., 160×160 vs 224×224), rendering the evidence insufficient to determine whether DeiT outperforms ViT when all factors are held constant.

response.study: We will re‑train ViT‑B/16 and DeiT‑B under a unified protocol: ImageNet‑1K only pre‑training, 224×224 resolution, 300 epochs, AdamW optimizer, standard data augmentation (random resized cropping, horizontal flip, MixUp, CutMix). Both models will be evaluated in three configurations: (i) non‑distilled baseline, (ii) DeiT‑style distillation with a ConvNet teacher (e.g., RegNetY‑8GF), and (iii) a ViT counterpart trained with the same distillation pipeline to assess whether the gains are attributable to the architecture or the distillation token. Each configuration will be run with five different random seeds; we will report mean top‑1 accuracy and 95 % confidence intervals. Additionally, we will ablate the number of pre‑training epochs to examine data‑efficiency: whether DeiT matches or exceeds ViT accuracy with fewer epochs while keeping all other factors equal. Limitations include the reliance on a single teacher architecture for distillation, the exclusion of external‑data pre‑training regimes (e.g., JFT‑300M) from the primary comparison, and the potential sensitivity to optimizer hyper‑parameters that were not exhaustively explored in the source papers.
